lead: A pilot's command must travel from the stick or pedal to a surface far away. Two mechanical ways do this. A push-pull rod is a tube that carries the command in both directions, push and pull, and needs bell cranks and guides to route it. A cable system carries only pull, so it always runs as a matched pair: one cable pulls the surface one way while the other slackens. Rods suit short, straight runs; cables suit long, curved runs. Both are still found on light aircraft and as the mechanical backbone of power-assisted airliners.
prereq: You need Chapter 1.1 for the cockpit controls and the surfaces they move.

sections.h3: Push-pull rod: a tube that takes both directions

blocks.text: A push-pull rod is a thin metal tube with an end fitting at each end. The fitting ends in a ball-jointed rod end: a spherical bearing inside a housing. The ball lets the rod tilt a few degrees without bending the tube, and it removes side loads. A rod carries tension when pulled and compression when pushed. Tension is easy; compression can make a long thin tube buckle sideways. The limit is set by Euler buckling, not by material strength.

blocks.where: P_cr is the critical buckling load in N; E is Young's modulus in Pa; I is the second moment of area of the tube section in m⁴; L is the unsupported length in m; K is the end-condition factor, about 1 for pin-ended rods.
σ is axial stress in Pa; F is axial force in N; A is cross-section area in m².

blocks.text: A bell crank is a two-armed lever on a pivot. It redirects the rod and can change the ratio of motion by unequal arm lengths. An idler lever only supports and redirects; it does not change the ratio. Guides and idler levers break a long run into short unsupported lengths, which raises the buckling load. Every joint adds backlash, a small lost motion. Temperature changes the rod length, so rigging must leave adjustment.

sections.h3: Cable and pulley: pull only, so always in pairs

blocks.text: Aircraft control cable is stranded steel: many thin wires twisted into strands, strands into a cable. It is flexible and strong in tension. It cannot push. So the surface is driven by a closed loop of two cables. When the pilot moves the control, one cable pulls the horn and the other cable goes slack. The slack cable is kept under pre-tension so it follows without lost motion when the direction reverses.

Pulleys redirect the cable. Fairleads are small guides that keep the cable in line through structure. At a pressurised bulkhead, a pressure seal lets the cable pass without leaking cabin air. A turnbuckle is a threaded link that shortens or lengthens the cable to set tension. A tension regulator is a spring-loaded device that keeps tension nearly constant as the aircraft expands with temperature and the cable stretches. Rigging pins lock the surfaces and controls at neutral while tensions are set.

A flexible push-pull cable is different: a stranded inner core slides inside a flexible conduit. It can follow a curved route and carries push and pull, but with more friction than a rod. It is common for throttle, mixture and other secondary controls.

blocks.where: ΔL is cable stretch in m; F is tension in N; L is cable length in m; A is the metal cross-section area in m²; E is Young's modulus in Pa.

blocks.text: Backlash, also called lost motion, is the small movement at a joint before the load is carried. Rods have backlash at each ball joint and bell crank bearing. Cables have stretch and pulley clearance. Backlash makes the control feel loose and can cause flutter if it grows.

Friction rises with every pulley and fairlead, so a long cable run can feel heavy. Rods have less friction but need straight lines and strong supports. A rod can jam if the structure bends into its path; a cable can jump a pulley or wear through a fairlead. Maintenance checks tension, pulley freedom, cable wear and rod-end play.

As aircraft grow faster and larger, the airload on a surface, and so the hinge moment, grows beyond a pilot's strength. Friction and stretch in a long cable run make the response imprecise. Rods add weight and need many bell cranks. The mechanical system still gives the command, but it needs help to supply the force. That help is the subject of Chapter 1.3.

examples.question: A rudder cable is 3 m long, of cross-section 6 mm², steel with E = 200 GPa, and the turnbuckle pre-tensions it to 1.5 kN. (a) Find the stretch. (b) A push-pull rod of the same length with cross-section 50 mm² carries the same 1.5 kN in compression; find the stress.
steps: Convert: cable area A_c = 6 mm² = 6 × 10⁻⁶ m²; E = 200 GPa = 200 × 10⁹ Pa; F = 1.5 kN = 1500 N; L = 3 m.
30 MPa is far below steel yield, so the rod does not fail by stress; it fails by buckling if the unsupported length is too large.
examples.answer: (a) Stretch = 3.75 mm. (b) Compressive stress = 30 MPa, so the rod's real limit is buckling, not stress.
examples.check:
F = 1500.0
L = 3.0
A_c = 6e-6
E = 200e9
dL = F * L / (A_c * E)
A_r = 50e-6
sigma = F / A_r
print(dL)
print(sigma)

traps: Drawing one cable that both pushes and pulls the surface. A cable can only pull, so the surface needs a second cable pulling the other way.
Checking a push-pull rod in compression by stress alone. A long thin rod fails by buckling at a load far below its stress limit.
Forgetting pre-tension in the return cable. A slack cable gives lost motion and a delayed response when the control reverses.
Confusing a bell crank with an idler lever. A bell crank redirects and can change the motion ratio; an idler only supports and redirects.
Mixing mm² and m² in ΔL = FL/(AE). Using 6 instead of 6 × 10⁻⁶ gives a stretch a million times too large.

quiz.q: What load can an aircraft control cable carry: tension, compression, or both?
quiz.a: Tension only. A cable cannot carry compression, so it must be used in a pair.

quiz.q: Why must a cable control run be a closed loop of two cables?
quiz.a: Because a cable can only pull. One cable pulls the surface in one direction; the second cable pulls it back in the other direction. The second cable is kept pre-tensioned so there is no lost motion.

quiz.q: A cable of length 2 m and cross-section 5 mm² is tensioned to 1 kN. Steel has E = 200 GPa. Find the stretch.
A long push-pull rod buckles in compression. Name two changes that raise its buckling load without changing the material.
quiz.a: Increase the tube diameter or second moment of area I. Shorten the unsupported length L by adding an idler lever or guide. Changing the end conditions to reduce K also helps.

quiz.q: What does a turnbuckle do in a cable system?
quiz.a: A turnbuckle is a threaded link that shortens or lengthens the cable run to set the correct tension and neutral position during rigging.

quiz.q: Why does a tension regulator help a cable system on a hot day?
quiz.a: Heat expands the airframe and changes cable length, so tension would change. A spring-loaded tension regulator absorbs the movement and keeps cable tension nearly constant, avoiding slack or overload.

quiz.q: A bell crank has an input arm of 50 mm and an output arm of 100 mm. The input rod moves 10 mm. Find the output movement.
quiz.a: Output movement = input × (output arm / input arm) = 10 × (100/50) = 20 mm, in the opposite direction. The output force is halved in the ideal case.

beyond: Not for the exam. Modern transports keep cables only as a backup or for secondary controls; the main path is fly-by-wire. Research looks at health monitoring of rod ends and cable tension sensors, and at replacing mechanical rigging with electrically signalled actuators. Search for 'control cable tension regulator', 'push-pull rod buckling aircraft' and 'fly-by-wire vs mechanical flight control'.
